prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: EN · Plan comparison (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 17px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Feature" · longest unbreakable word 63px · one-line width 93px
  col 2: header "Free" · longest unbreakable word 88px · one-line width 88px
  col 3: header "Pro" · longest unbreakable word 73px · one-line width 73px
  col 4: header "Enterprise" · longest unbreakable word 83px · one-line width 255px
  col 5: header "Notes" · longest unbreakable word 81px · one-line width 465px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 643px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 642px.
Fixed: content, font, 17px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"bad","why":"Words break mid-token — \"Unlimite d\" in Pro and \"Communit y\" in Free — because those columns were sized below their longest unbreakable word; the table reads as damaged text."},"B":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Feature labels stay on one line, Free/Pro/Enterprise are compact but never break a word, and Notes gets ~190px so the prose reads in three clean lines; column rhythm tracks content."},"C":{"grade":"poor","why":"Notes is starved to ~110px, stacking the prose into 5–7 ragged lines, while Free/Pro/Enterprise sit on wide near-empty fields — effort is spent on the columns that need it least."},"D":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Overall balanced and no word is broken, but the first column is too narrow: \"SSO / SAML\" wraps to two lines, so row labels stop reading as consistent single-line units."},"E":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Effectively B with a slightly wider Notes; plan columns stay tight, all words and labels intact, and the prose column carries its weight without stealing from the numbers."},"F":{"grade":"good","why":"Sound and unbroken, but Enterprise is trimmed enough that \"24/7 phone & dedicated manager\" breaks into three short lines while Notes gains slack it does not need — a mild inversion of emphasis."}},"best":["B","E"],"confidence":"medium","unsure":"B and E are nearly identical at this resolution (only a few px of Notes/Enterprise differ), so I cannot reliably separate them; D's narrow label column may be a deliberate row-label treatment rather than an error."}
